reason: The source unit is the permit, but the dependence unit is the construction project or development site: the release itself states that permits sharing ParentPermitNum, RelatedMUP or a development site are correlated and that no row independence is claimed (README.md:58,67; construction.json:278,424). The project keys are not shipped: carry_columns is empty (construction.json:37) and the linking fields are reduced to presence flags (build.py:205-206), so permitnum, although unique (build.py:243-244), would treat sibling permits as independent. issueddate is a shipped non-predictor carry (build.py:31, absent from FEATURES at build.py:21-30), is the declared event key and split key (construction.json:36,70), and is the issuance event at which sibling permits of one project are commonly released together. In public train, a label-free same-day signature (issue day, ZIP level, class, type, description length, application-to-issue days) places 6.0% of rows in multi-permit groups, 48% of which carry parent_permit_flag=1 versus 3.4% elsewhere; 88% of those groups have a unanimous label versus 57% expected under independence (within-group ICC 0.68). Every such group nests inside one issue day, so issue-day clusters contain the observed sibling dependence plus any same-day administrative batch effect. Train label ICC by issue day is 0.022 at about 13 rows per day (design effect about 1.27); public validation gives 0.014 (about 1.15). Train has 856 issue-day clusters over 36 months and validation 625 over 24 months, so the 21-month holdout window should supply several hundred clusters. Chosen from source meaning plus public train and validation data only, before holdout scoring; no holdout rows or holdout metrics were inspected.
limitations: issueddate is an issuance-day block, not the project entity. The true entity keys (ParentPermitNum, RelatedMUP, address, contractor) are not in the released extract, so project-level clustering cannot be applied or verified.

Sibling permits issued on different days fall in different clusters. Among train rows with parent_permit_flag=1, a looser date-free signature finds 41 groups (123 rows) spanning different issue days (median span 258 days, maximum 975) with 76% unanimous labels, so some project dependence escapes this clustering and can cross split boundaries. That signature is a weak proxy and may include coincidental matches.

Issue-day clusters also pool unrelated permits issued the same day (median 12 rows per day, maximum 60 in train). This widens clusters beyond the project but does not restore independence across days.

Common shocks at month or year scale are not absorbed: train label rates drift by issue year (0.818, 0.752, 0.765) and outcome windows of train, validation and holdout overlap in calendar time. Intervals from issue-day clustering describe sampling within this regime, not transfer to another period.
Dependence through repeat applicants, contractors or sites over time is not captured; those identifiers were dropped from the release for terms-of-use reasons (README.md:55).
The holdout cluster count and cluster-size distribution are extrapolated from train and validation density and were not checked against holdout rows.

The same-day signature used as evidence is a heuristic built from shipped feature columns. It was used only to assess dependence, is not proposed as a cluster key, and true project membership was not verified against the raw source.
